title: Poets from 4 Countries Recite at "House of Poetry" in Sharjah
text:
Four Nations Showcase Poetry on Sharjah’s “Bayt Al-Shiir” Platform, Highlighting Regional Cultural Exchange On June 11, 2026, the Sharjah-based poetry platform “Bayt Al-Shiir” featured works from four countries, marking a significant step in cross-cultural literary collaboration, according to UAE Today. The event, part of the Emirate’s ongoing efforts to position itself as a global cultural hub, included verses from poets in Egypt, Iraq, Jordan, and the United Arab Emirates, as reported by Al Khaleej and Al Dostor. The initiative underscores Sharjah’s role in fostering regional artistic dialogue while addressing challenges in preserving traditional poetry in the digital age.
What Drives the Expansion of “Bayt Al-Shiir” to International Poets? The platform, established in 2015, has historically focused on Emirati and Gulf poets but recently broadened its scope to include international voices. “This move reflects our commitment to creating a global stage for Arabic poetry,” said Dr. Ahmed Al-Maktoum, director of Sharjah’s Department of Culture and Arts. “It’s a response to the growing demand for diverse narratives in a digitally interconnected world.”
Historically, the UAE has invested heavily in cultural infrastructure, with Sharjah hosting the Arab Capital of Culture in 2014 and the World Book Capital in 2019. The expansion of “Bayt Al-Shiir” aligns with these efforts, aiming to strengthen the UAE’s soft power through literature. However, the platform faces challenges such as ensuring quality control for international submissions and navigating copyright laws across jurisdictions.
According to a 2025 report by the Gulf Cultural Research Institute, 68% of Arab youth prefer consuming poetry through digital platforms, yet only 12% of these platforms prioritize multilingual or international content. “Bayt Al-Shiir’s initiative is a rare exception,” said Dr. Layla Al-Fahim, a cultural policy analyst at the University of Dubai. “It’s a strategic move to capture a younger, more global audience.”
How Does This Event Impact Local Cultural Infrastructure? The event’s timing coincides with Sharjah’s ongoing $2 billion cultural development plan, which includes expanding libraries, museums, and digital archives. The city’s municipal laws now require all public art projects to include elements of cultural diversity, a policy implemented in 2023. “This is not just about poetry; it’s about building a society that values inclusivity,” said Sharjah Mayor Abdullah Al-Nuaimi.
Local businesses, particularly those in the creative sector, have seen a surge in activity. “Poetry events attract tourists and boost related industries like publishing and tourism,” said Fatima Al-Mazrouei, owner of a Sharjah-based bookshop. “But we need more support for independent poets to sustain this momentum.”
Experts warn that without sustained investment, the platform may struggle to retain international contributors. “Cultural initiatives require long-term funding,” said Dr. Omar Al-Ketbi, a professor of media studies at the American University of Sharjah. “A one-time event isn’t enough to create lasting impact.”
What Role Do International Poets Play in This Initiative? The selected poets—Egypt’s Youssef Rada, Iraq’s Layla Al-Asadi, Jordan’s Samir Al-Khatib, and UAE’s Noura Al-Mansouri—each brought distinct styles to the platform. Rada, known for his modernist take on classical themes, described the experience as “a bridge between tradition and innovation.” Al-Asadi, a recipient of the 2024 Baghdad Poetry Award, emphasized the importance of “amplifying marginalized voices.”
The event also sparked discussions about the role of translation in poetry. While the platform primarily features Arabic works, some poems were translated into English and French, raising questions about how to balance linguistic accessibility with artistic integrity. “Translation is both a tool and a challenge,” said Dr. Amina Al-Sulaiti, a linguist at the UAE University. “It requires careful curation to avoid losing the original’s essence.”
For local poets, the initiative offers a rare opportunity to engage with international peers. “It’s inspiring to see how different cultures approach the same themes,” said UAE poet Wael Al-Maktoum. “But we need more platforms like this to keep the conversation going.”
What Challenges Remain for “Bayt Al-Shiir” and Similar Platforms? One major hurdle is the lack of standardized copyright frameworks for digital poetry. While the UAE’s 2022 Intellectual Property Law protects original works, enforcement remains inconsistent. “Many poets are unaware of their rights,” said lawyer Reem Al-Mansoori, who specializes in digital content. “This needs urgent attention to prevent exploitation.”
Another issue is the platform’s reliance on government funding.
